I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5: hackertube.org/ - Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session) - Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads - Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version - HackerTube Longs ✊ A bit more on the process: I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing. Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

If you've ever wondered why smart TVs are so cheap, this is why. @log4j rooted his Samsung and found an always-on hot mic, automatic content recognition, geolocation, network mapping, ad targeting and user profiling, shared with Samsung's "400 partners". A lot of it can be blocked in <15 min, wrote a basic guide below. What your TV is doing The main culprit is ACR (automatic content recognition). Your TV screenshots what's on screen, fingerprints it, and sends it home to build your ad profile. Samsung does it every 500ms, LG every 10ms [1]. What is insane: it happens on connected devices too. Plug in your laptop, your console, your work machine, and your TV can fingerprint that via HDMI [1]. He also found that if your Samsung doesn't have a mic, it'll look for one from a connected soundbar or bluetooth device. nitterk.kareem.one/log4j/status/211376224… It's on by default, and you likely agreed to it on the setup screen you clicked through in 10 seconds. Step 1: Turn off ACR Samsung: Terms & Privacy → Viewing Information Services LG: Live Plus Vizio: Viewing Data Roku: "Use info from TV inputs" Sony/Google TV: Samba Interactive TV Menus vary by model, but those are the names to look for. While you're in there, opt out of interest-based ads, reset your advertising ID, decline every optional privacy agreement, turn off voice recognition, and delete apps you never open. Step 2: Give smart devices their own network Put the TV, cameras, speakers and vacuum on your router's guest/IoT network. The logic is simple: these devices rarely get patched. If one gets compromised (getting drastically more frequent with AI), it shouldn't be able to see your other devices or home network. Step 3: Block trackers for the whole house with DNS-level filtering NextDNS (cloud-based) is easy and has a solid free plan. Pi-hole is a little bit more work if you prefer self hosting. For simplicity we'll focus on the former. 1. Sign up at nextdns.io (free tier is plenty) 2. Privacy tab: add a blocklist (OISD is a good bet) and turn on Native Tracking Protection for Samsung, LG, Roku, Amazon (see attached image) 3. Setup tab: copy your endpoint 4. Paste it into your router's DNS settings as DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS (or use the IPs + "Link IP" if your router only does plain DNS) 5. Bonus: block outbound port 53 except to your router. Some devices hardcode their own DNS to get around you Then open the NextDNS logs and watch how often your TV phones home. It's eye-opening. If an app or update breaks, find the domain in the logs and allowlist it. Why they do this TV prices are down 97% since 2000 [2]. Most of that is better manufacturing and brutal competition. But once margins on the hardware hit zero, the cost moved to you. In Q3 2024, Vizio lost $6.7M selling TVs and made $115.8M in gross profit from ads and viewing data [3]. They've said on earnings calls that they keep TV prices low to grow the audience they sell to advertisers. Walmart bought them in 2024. This isn't a conspiracy theory either. Vizio paid $2.2M to the FTC in 2017 for tracking 11 million TVs without consent. Last December, Texas sued Samsung, LG, Sony, Hisense and TCL over ACR. Samsung and LG have since agreed to stop collecting that data without explicit consent [4]. TL;DR 1. ACR off 2. Ads + voice off 3. Smart devices on their own network 4. NextDNS filtering on the router Sources: [1] ACR study: arxiv.org/abs/2409.06203 [2] Cost of US consumer goods: aei.org/economics/chart-of-t… [3] Vizio Q3 2024: sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… [4] Texas v. Samsung: texasattorneygeneral.gov/new… log4j (@log4j) i own a relatively new (2025) samsung tv. i kept getting weirdly targeted ads. i tried reversing the firmware but it was aes encrypted and no keys unless tear it apart and do uart/jtag magic. zero days it is. root shell on new samsung TVs! discovered PRIVACY HORROR. write up? — https://nitter.kareem.one/log4j/status/2113014142600953868#m

Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability. The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly, this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along. So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions. TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge), but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are. — https://nitter.kareem.one/karpathy/status/2042334451611693415#m

We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks: Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better: Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better: Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better: Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work! In summary: - As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding. - Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

processed.summary: Aujourd'hui, le monde de l'IA nous montre des avancées pratiques et des réflexions profondes. D'un côté, de nouveaux outils et modèles d'IA génératrice d'images sont désormais accessibles pour créer des GIFs ou éditer plus facilement, et des applications astucieuses comme HackerTube voient le jour grâce à l'IA. D'un autre côté, les experts soulignent un fossé croissant dans la compréhension des capacités réelles de l'IA, allant du simple chatbot à des systèmes autonomes résolvant des problèmes complexes, tout en nous alertant sur l'importance de la vie privée face aux technologies comme les Smart TV.

glossaire.definition: Modèle de langage avancé capable de comprendre, générer et traiter du texte de manière très complexe.
Un système d'intelligence artificielle capable d'agir de manière autonome pour atteindre des objectifs, parfois en interagissant avec son environnement.
Un ensemble de règles et d'outils qui permet à différents logiciels de communiquer entre eux, par exemple pour qu'une application utilise un service d'IA.
Un type d'IA qui essaie de simuler et de prédire le fonctionnement d'un environnement réel ou virtuel, pour mieux comprendre les conséquences de ses actions.
Technologie qui identifie automatiquement le contenu affiché sur un écran de télévision, souvent utilisée pour collecter des données sur les habitudes de visionnage.
Une méthode d'entraînement pour les IA où elles apprennent à prendre de bonnes décisions en recevant des 'récompenses' ou des 'pénalités' pour leurs actions.
La plus petite unité de texte (comme un mot, une partie de mot ou un signe de ponctuation) que les modèles d'IA traitent et génèrent.

category_summaries.actu: Les actualités du jour mettent en lumière le déploiement de nouveaux modèles d'IA puissants comme Gemini 4 Carbon, spécialisé en cybersécurité, et un aperçu du modèle de monde Genie 4. Elles révèlent aussi l'incroyable demande pour ces "intelligences" et des progrès en matière d'efficacité pour certains modèles textuels.
category_summaries.tips: Cette catégorie offre des conseils concrets pour le lecteur, comme un guide détaillé pour protéger sa vie privée face aux collectes de données des Smart TV. Elle propose également des méthodes pour mieux interagir avec les IA et obtenir des explications claires, via des formats comme des diagrammes ou des pages web interactives.
category_summaries.idees: Les discussions d'aujourd'hui portent sur la perception très inégale des capacités de l'IA entre le grand public et les experts, l'importance pour les futurs agents IA de pouvoir prédire les conséquences de leurs actions (une critique des LLM actuels), ainsi que la manière dont les entreprises s'adaptent à l'IA et comment les modèles interprètent les symboles visuels.
category_summaries.outils: Plusieurs outils innovants sont désormais disponibles : un système de recommandations vidéo (HackerTube) créé par IA, et surtout, des mises à jour majeures des modèles d'images d'OpenAI (Images 2.6, Flare, Sunburst) permettant de générer des images plus rapidement, de créer des GIFs animés, et de réutiliser des images de référence dans ChatGPT et via API.

C'est maintenant moins "deux groupes de personnes qui parlent sans se comprendre" et plus un entonnoir aigu. - Selon des estimations rapides, environ 6 milliards de personnes (~75% de la population) n'ont quasiment pas eu de contact avec les LLM. - Environ 1-2 milliards (~20%) sont des utilisateurs occasionnels et peu fréquents de produits gratuits de type ChatGPT. Step 1: Turn off ACR Samsung: Terms & Privacy → Viewing Information Services LG: Live Plus Vizio: Viewing Data Roku: "Use info from TV inputs" Sony/Google TV: Samba Interactive TV Menus vary by model, but those are the names to look for. While you're in there, opt out of interest-based ads, reset your advertising ID, decline every optional privacy agreement, turn off voice recognition, and delete apps you never open. Step 2: Give smart devices their own network Put the TV, cameras, speakers and vacuum on your router's guest/IoT network. The logic is simple: these devices rarely get patched. Step 3: Block trackers for the whole house with DNS-level filtering NextDNS (cloud-based) is easy and has a solid free plan. Pi-hole is a little bit more work if you prefer self hosting. For simplicity we'll focus on the former. 1. Sign up at nextdns.io (free tier is plenty) 2. Privacy tab: add a blocklist (OISD is a good bet) and turn on Native Tracking Protection for Samsung, LG, Roku, Amazon (see attached image) 3. Setup tab: copy your endpoint 4. tips.text_fr: Nous allons passer beaucoup plus de temps à essayer de comprendre les sorties des modèles de langage. Quelques réflexions, astuces & conseils : Écriture. Les LLM connaissent bien ce langage et il impose des contraintes strictes sur un style d'écriture clair que je trouve souvent beaucoup plus lisible. Parfois, j'ai essayé de l'adoucir un peu, par exemple en demandant "80% du chemin vers ASD-STE100" car la spécification est assez rigoureuse. Mais encore mieux : Diagrammes / images. Au lieu d'écrire, demandez à votre LLM de créer un diagramme. Ceux-ci peuvent être beaucoup plus faciles à traiter, analyser et comprendre. Mais encore mieux : Pages web. Demandez une sortie "en HTML" pour obtenir une page web interactive et esthétique. Les LLM sont de plus en plus doués pour le frontend et peuvent créer de belles expériences, des animations, etc. Mais encore mieux : Vidéos explicatives. Le format de sortie pour lequel je suis le plus optimiste est les vidéos explicatives entièrement personnalisées / sur mesure générées sur n'importe quel sujet arbitraire. Expérimentez avec des choses comme "Créez une vidéo explicative de style 3b1b sur X. Utilisez ma clé API ElevenLabs pour la narration audio". (vous auriez besoin d'une clé API pour cette dernière ou vous pouvez demander à votre LLM de vous trouver des alternatives gratuites décentes qui utilisent votre calcul local). Cela commence vraiment à fonctionner ! En résumé : - À mesure que les LLM s'améliorent, ils feront de plus en plus de travail de manière autonome, et une grande partie de notre travail s'élèvera dans les abstractions vers la supervision et la compréhension. - Heureusement, les LLM peuvent aussi aider ici car à mesure que l'intelligence et le code deviennent de plus en plus abondants, vous pouvez demander de grands artefacts logiciels personnalisés et jetables (par exemple, des applications web, des vidéos explicatives) qu'il n'aurait jamais été logique de créer auparavant. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better: Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better: Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better: Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). idees.text_fr: Je dépoussière ce tweet d'avril parce que cet écart de compréhension partagée de la capacité des LLM *s'élargit*. C'est maintenant moins "deux groupes de personnes qui parlent sans se comprendre" et plus un entonnoir aigu. - Selon des estimations rapides, environ 6 milliards de personnes (~75% de la population) n'ont quasiment pas eu de contact avec les LLM. - Environ 1-2 milliards (~20%) sont des utilisateurs occasionnels et peu fréquents de produits gratuits de type ChatGPT. Ce groupe voit des chatbots un peu maladroits et les traite comme une meilleure recherche Google, une aide à l'écriture, etc. Peut-être qu'un agent essaie de vous réserver un vol. J'ai des amis non-tech qui (raisonnablement, selon moi) disent ne pas en avoir beaucoup l'utilité. Même de nombreux professionnels en dehors des mathématiques et du code sont à ce niveau. Par exemple, les dirigeants et de nombreuses autres fonctions passent une grande partie de leur temps à parler à d'autres personnes, donc même s'ils comprennent intellectuellement ce qui se passe, c'est encore de seconde main et un peu abstrait. - Maintenant, nous arrivons à l'utilisation professionnelle des LLM de pointe en mathématiques et en code. Environ 20 millions de personnes (0,2%) voient de leurs propres yeux que de grands projets complexes qui leur prenaient des semaines/mois peuvent maintenant être réalisés par des agents avec un simple prompt. Construire des applications, copier des applications, traduire des applications, décompiler des applications à partir de binaires... Tout cela s'est produit très rapidement et récemment - il y a moins d'un an, j'écrivais du code manuellement, en tapant des commandes informatiques mémorisées caractère par caractère dans un éditeur de code, appuyant occasionnellement sur Tab pour compléter un petit morceau de code. - Et enfin, nous arrivons aux environ 5 000 personnes (~0,00006%) ayant accès à des systèmes de pointe en interne. Le monde extérieur a vu l'aperçu. Cela ressemble à des essaims de milliers d'agents collaborant pendant des semaines sur des mégaprojets logiciels : création de "zero days", exécution de cyberattaques et de défenses à la vitesse de la machine, découverte de nouvelles sciences, avancement de la frontière des mathématiques. Des choses qui auraient pris des années de travail aux meilleurs professionnels de l'industrie. Pendant ce temps, la révision et la compréhension humaines commencent à prendre du retard. Par exemple, les gens sont encore impliqués dans "l'archéologie" de l'incident OpenAI-HF d'il y a plusieurs mois. Les mathématiciens peuvent passer un certain temps à examiner les 722 manuscrits sur les mathématiques de pointe. L'entonnoir est lié à une combinaison de facteurs : 1. L'impact est proportionnel à l'ambition, à la taille du problème et à l'horizon. Une question avec une réponse d'un paragraphe stresse à peine le système. Vous avez besoin d'un réservoir de problèmes grands et difficiles qui vous tiennent vraiment à cœur. Cet aspect pilote la dimension consommateur / professionnel de l'entonnoir. 2. La rugosité du système (sur laquelle j'ai beaucoup écrit séparément). La capacité atteint des sommets dans des domaines numériques, vérifiables et économiquement précieux. C'est parce que la capacité des LLM émerge de l'apprentissage par renforcement sur des récompenses vérifiables dans un mélange d'environnements géré par le potentiel de revenus. Cet aspect pilote principalement la dimension du domaine (par exemple, mathématiques et code) de l'entonnoir. 3. Accès. Gratuit, payant, interne. C'est donc la particularité du moment. Le grand public n'a pour la plupart pas interagi avec ces systèmes. Quand ils l'ont fait, cela ressemble à un chatbot un peu nigaud. La majorité des professionnels ne voient encore qu'une amélioration modeste. Et une petite tranche de professionnels vit le vertige de la courbe qui monte verticalement. Et il est simultanément vrai que le "mode vocal avancé" gratuit et je pense un peu orphelin (?) d'OpenAI va gâcher les questions les plus stupides dans vos vidéos Instagram et *en même temps*, le modèle payant et de plus haut niveau d'OpenAI, Codex, va passer 1 heure à restructurer de manière cohérente une base de code entière, ou à trouver et exploiter des vulnérabilités dans des systèmes informatiques. Cette partie fonctionne vraiment et a fait des progrès spectaculaires grâce à 2 propriétés : 1) ces domaines offrent des fonctions de récompense explicites et vérifiables, ce qui signifie qu'ils sont facilement adaptables à l'apprentissage par renforcement (par exemple, tests unitaires passés oui ou non, contrairement à l'écriture, qui est beaucoup plus difficile à juger explicitement), mais aussi 2) ils sont beaucoup plus précieux dans les contextes B2B, ce qui signifie que la plus grande partie de l'équipe se concentre sur leur amélioration.
idees.text_original: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability. The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly, this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along. So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions. TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge), but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them.
